name: Rules Students Can Follow
title: Rules Students Can Follow
answer: A district's acceptable use policy for AI works best when it is written in plain language that students and parents can follow, and when each assignment carries a clear level of allowed AI use. This matters because outright bans push AI use out of sight while informal guidelines create inconsistent rules from classroom to classroom. Marking the allowed level on the assignment itself turns the question from whether AI was used into whether it was used as permitted.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: This idea is an acceptable use policy for AI that a district drafts with teachers, students, and parents and reviews every year. It solves the problem that many districts first tried either banning student use or relying on a few informal guidelines, and both proved hard to sustain. A ban drives use underground rather than preventing it, and informal guidelines mean each classroom operates under different expectations. The policy's most useful piece is a simple scale of allowed AI use that the teacher marks on each assignment, so no one has to guess what is permitted. A research paper, for example, might be marked for feedback on a draft only, while a brainstorming exercise might allow AI for generating ideas.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the teacher selects a level from the scale and marks it directly on the assignment, so students know before they begin what AI use is allowed. The book describes a five level scale that works from upper elementary through high school, so the same structure can carry across grade bands even as the assignments change. A research paper might sit at the level that permits AI feedback on a draft only, while a brainstorming exercise might sit at a level that allows AI for ideas. Because the level travels with the assignment, the rule is visible at the moment of the work rather than buried in a district document. This replaces the guessing that comes with informal guidelines and the inconsistency of different rules in every classroom.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea as practice based rather than research based. It reports that many districts started with a ban on student use or a few informal guidelines and then found both hard to sustain, citing McGuire et al., 2026. The text also states that AI detection scores are not proof, which is the reason the scale avoids leaning on them. Figure 3.7 in the book shows the five level scale that works from upper elementary through high school. No further studies or figures are given for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are practical and human. A ban pushes use out of sight, and informal guidelines produce different rules in every classroom, so neither is a safe default. The policy has to be drafted with teachers, students, and parents and reviewed each year, which keeps the decisions in human hands rather than fixed once and forgotten. The scale shifts the conversation away from whether a student used AI and toward whether the student used it at the level the assignment allowed, which is the fairer question. Teachers still decide the level for each assignment, and the text warns against relying on AI detection scores because they are not proof.
